# Machine Translation {#sec-machine-translation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number on this page was measured on WMT16
newstest2016 Turkish–English — 3,000 professionally translated sentence pairs
in each direction, downloaded by `sacrebleu` itself so that the test set is
identified rather than described. Systems are scored on the first 1,000
sentences, the LLM on the first 400, stated where it appears.
@sec-machine-translation-turkish measures why the field's default metric is
harsher on Turkish than on English, using the same semantic error in both
languages. Software: `sacrebleu` 2.6.0, `transformers` 5.15.1, PyTorch 2.13.0
on Python 3.14.5; the MT model on an Apple M-series GPU, the LLM through
`ollama` 0.24.0.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain why translation is the task that produced the attention mechanism,
  and what the bottleneck was that attention removed;
- pick a decoding strategy suited to translation rather than to chat, and say
  why the same setting is right in one and wrong in the other;
- compute BLEU by hand, state precisely what it can and cannot see, and
  report it alongside something that sees more;
- quantify why a word-level metric is harsher on an agglutinative language
  than on English, rather than asserting that it is;
- decide between a dedicated MT model and an LLM on measured quality, latency
  and cost;
- choose between translate-train, translate-test and neither, and say where
  the errors accumulate in each.

## Translation is where attention came from {#sec-machine-translation-attention}

@sec-transformers taught attention as a mechanism. This chapter is where it
gets its origin story, because attention was not invented as a general idea —
it was invented to fix one specific, measurable failure in translation.

The 2014 architecture [@sutskever2014sequence] was an encoder RNN that read
the source sentence and compressed it into **a single fixed-length vector**,
and a decoder RNN that generated the translation from that vector alone.
Elegant, and it worked — up to a point that was easy to find. Everything the
decoder would ever know about a forty-word sentence had to fit in the same
number of floats as everything it would know about a four-word one.

The symptom was unmistakable: [translation quality fell off a cliff as source
sentences got longer]{.hl}, and it fell off in a specific way — the model
would translate the beginning and then drift, because the end of the source
had overwritten the start of the vector.

@bahdanau2015neural's fix was to stop compressing. Keep one vector per source
token, and let the decoder, at each output step, compute a weighted average
over all of them — weights that depend on what it is currently trying to
produce. That is attention, and the reason it was obviously right here is
that translation has a property the mechanism mirrors exactly: **output words
correspond to input words**. When the decoder emits *Istanbul*, the useful
information is concentrated in one source position, and an average that can
concentrate its weight there is a better interface than a fixed summary.

::: {.column-margin}
This is why the first attention papers could publish alignment heatmaps that
looked like word alignments — and why later attempts to read transformer
attention heads as explanations disappointed. In a translation encoder-decoder
the alignment interpretation is *earned* by the task's structure. In a
24-layer language model it is a hypothesis, and usually a wrong one.
:::

Three years later @vaswani2017attention removed the recurrence and kept only
the attention, which is @sec-transformers' subject. The lineage is worth
holding on to: the dominant architecture in machine learning began as a repair
to a translation bug.

## Three eras, and what each got right {#sec-machine-translation-history}

**Statistical MT** [@brown1993mathematics; @koehn2003statistical] learned a
phrase table — *this source phrase maps to that target phrase with this
probability* — plus a target-language model to keep the output fluent, and a
reordering model. It was assembled from parts you could inspect. If a
translation was wrong you could find the phrase-table entry responsible and
read it.

[Word alignment is the thing worth carrying forward from that era.]{.hl} It
was the last time the field had a fully interpretable account of what a
translation system was doing, and it is still what terminology enforcement,
translation memories and localisation QA are built on. A system that cannot
say which source words produced which target words cannot be audited by a
human translator, and in regulated localisation that is a hard requirement.

**Neural MT** replaced the pipeline with one trained model. It fixed
reordering and fluency almost immediately — statistical output read like
statistical output — and it introduced failure modes the phrase table could
not have: fluent inventions, dropped clauses, and a habit of translating a
rare word by whatever plausible thing it saw in training instead.
@koehn2017six catalogued them.

**General-purpose LLMs** were not built to translate and translate anyway,
because a next-token model trained on a multilingual web has seen the same
content in many languages. What they add over a dedicated model is *context*:
a document-level view, a glossary in the prompt, a register instruction. What
they lose is cost and determinism, and @sec-machine-translation-llm measures
both.

## Evaluation, and how BLEU actually works {#sec-machine-translation-eval}

Translation has no single right answer, so every automatic metric compares
against one or more human translations and reports a similarity. The metric
you pick decides which systems you will believe are better, so it is worth
knowing exactly what each one counts.

### BLEU by hand

[BLEU](#gloss-bleu){#term-bleu .term-ref} [@papineni2002bleu] is modified
n-gram precision, geometrically averaged over n = 1..4, multiplied by a
brevity penalty. That is the whole definition, and it fits in a worked
example.

::: {#gloss-bleu .column-margin .term-gloss}
**BLEU** — the share of the candidate's word n-grams that appear in the
reference, averaged over n = 1 to 4, with a penalty for being too short. The
field's default metric since 2002, and blind to any correct paraphrase that
uses different words. [↩](#term-bleu){.term-back}
:::

```text
REF: In Istanbul , heavy rain caused flooding on Monday evening .   (11 tokens)
HYP: Heavy rain in Istanbul caused flooding on Monday evening .     (10 tokens)
```

The candidate is a *correct translation*. It moved the location phrase to the
middle, which English permits and which changes nothing about the meaning.
Here is what BLEU makes of it:

```text
  1-gram precision   8/10 = 0.8000
  2-gram precision   5/9  = 0.5556
  3-gram precision   4/8  = 0.5000
  4-gram precision   3/7  = 0.4286

  brevity penalty    len(hyp)=10, len(ref)=11  ->  exp(1 - 11/10) = 0.9048
  geometric mean of the four precisions        =  0.5555

  BLEU = 0.9048 x 0.5555 = 50.27
```

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Edit the translation and watch BLEU move</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bleuRef = Inputs.text({label: "reference",
  value: "In Istanbul , heavy rain caused flooding on Monday evening .", width: 560})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bleuHyp = Inputs.text({label: "candidate",
  value: "Heavy rain in Istanbul caused flooding on Monday evening .", width: 560})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bleuLower = Inputs.toggle({label: "lowercase both first", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bleuScore = {
  const prep = t => (bleuLower ? t.toLowerCase() : t).trim().split(/\s+/).filter(x => x);
  const ref = prep(bleuRef), hyp = prep(bleuHyp);
  const grams = (a, n) => a.slice(0, Math.max(0, a.length - n + 1))
                           .map((_, i) => a.slice(i, i + n).join(" "));
  const rows = [];
  let logsum = 0;
  for (let n = 1; n <= 4; n++) {
    const h = grams(hyp, n), r = grams(ref, n);
    const need = new Map();
    for (const g of r) need.set(g, (need.get(g) ?? 0) + 1);   // clipped counts
    let hit = 0;
    for (const g of h) if ((need.get(g) ?? 0) > 0) { hit++; need.set(g, need.get(g) - 1); }
    const p = h.length ? hit / h.length : 0;
    rows.push({n: `${n}-gram`, matched: hit, total: h.length, precision: p});
    logsum += Math.log(Math.max(p, 1e-12));
  }
  const bp = hyp.length > ref.length ? 1 : Math.exp(1 - ref.length / Math.max(hyp.length, 1));
  const geo = Math.exp(logsum / 4);
  return {rows, bp, geo, bleu: bp * geo * 100, hlen: hyp.length, rlen: ref.length};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(bleuScore.rows, {
  columns: ["n", "matched", "total", "precision"],
  header: {n: "order", matched: "matched", total: "in candidate", precision: "precision"},
  format: {precision: v => v.toFixed(4)},
  width: {n: 90, matched: 90, total: 110, precision: 100},
  rows: 4})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`brevity penalty **${bleuScore.bp.toFixed(4)}** (candidate ${bleuScore.hlen}
tokens, reference ${bleuScore.rlen}) × geometric mean
**${bleuScore.geo.toFixed(4)}** = **BLEU ${bleuScore.bleu.toFixed(2)}**`
```
:::

**50.27 for a correct translation.** Two things did the damage, and both are
worth naming because they recur constantly:

- Moving *in Istanbul* broke every n-gram that crossed the move. The unigrams
  survived; the 4-grams did not.
- `Heavy` did not match `heavy`, and `in` did not match `In`. BLEU is
  case-sensitive by default. That alone cost two unigrams out of ten.

For the same pair, **chrF scores 83.23**, because at the character level
almost everything still matches.

::: {.column-margin}
Reproduce it and you will get 50.27 exactly — but only if you say which BLEU.
Tokenization, casing, and smoothing all change the number, which is why
`sacrebleu` exists and why @post2018call had to be written: a BLEU score
without its signature is not comparable to another BLEU score. Report the
signature, always.
:::

### The metric family, and what each one sees

| metric | unit | sees | misses |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| [BLEU](#gloss-bleu){.term-ref} | word n-grams | exact phrase matches | any paraphrase; partially-correct words |
| [chrF](#gloss-chrf){#term-chrf .term-ref} [@popovic2015chrf] | character n-grams | partially-correct words, morphology | meaning; a fluent sentence built of right characters |
| [COMET](#gloss-comet){#term-comet .term-ref} [@rei2020comet] | learned | meaning, as far as its training data taught it | anything its training data did not contain; and it needs a GPU |
| Human MQM [@freitag2021experts] | annotated errors | everything, by category and severity | nothing — it just costs money and days |

: Four ways to score a translation {tbl-colwidths="[16,16,34,34]"}

::: {#gloss-chrf .column-margin .term-gloss}
**chrF** — the same precision-and-recall idea as BLEU, computed over
character n-grams instead of word n-grams. Gives partial credit for a word
whose stem is right and whose ending is wrong, which is exactly the case an
agglutinative language produces constantly.
[↩](#term-chrf){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-comet .column-margin .term-gloss}
**COMET** — a neural metric: a model fine-tuned to predict human quality
judgements from the source, the hypothesis and the reference. Correlates far
better with humans than BLEU, and inherits every bias of the judgements it was
trained on. [↩](#term-comet){.term-back}
:::

The 2026 consensus, and the one this chapter follows: **report chrF and a
neural metric; report BLEU as well because everyone else does; never rank
systems on BLEU alone.** @kocmi2024navigating is the current guidance on how
large a difference in each metric has to be before it means anything.

## Decoding for translation {#sec-machine-translation-decoding}

@sec-decoding will argue that sampling is what you want for open-ended
generation. Translation is the counterexample, and the contrast is worth
having concretely rather than as a rule of thumb.

The difference is in the task. Open-ended generation has many good answers and
you want variety, so sampling from the distribution is the point. Translation
has approximately one good answer, you want the highest-probability sequence,
and variety is a defect. So translation uses **beam search**: keep the *k*
best partial hypotheses at each step and extend all of them, instead of
committing to the single best token.

Here is the whole decoding space on 500 sentences of newstest2016 tr-en with
`opus-mt-tc-big-tr-en`:

```text
kind      value    BLEU    chrF  len ratio  ms/sent
beam          1   29.45   58.01      1.015       51
beam          2   30.06   58.36      1.021       66
beam          4   30.17   58.41      1.022       80
beam          8   30.23   58.42      1.021      119
beam         16   30.25   58.41      1.022      166
beam         32   30.36   58.44      1.020      273
beam         64   30.63   58.58      1.018      459

lenpen      0.2   30.51   58.30      1.007       76
lenpen      0.6   30.44   58.42      1.013       74
lenpen      1.0   30.17   58.41      1.022       73
lenpen      1.4   29.83   58.37      1.031       75
lenpen      2.0   29.25   58.39      1.041       74

sample      0.3   28.95   57.42      1.016       45
sample      0.7   25.90   55.17      1.013       45
sample      1.0   14.34   45.27      1.111       53
```

### Sampling is a disaster here

**BLEU 30.17 at beam 4 against 14.34 at temperature 1.0.** The same model,
the same sentences; the decoder threw away half the quality. Pure sampling
picks a token proportional to its probability, so on every token there is a
chance of taking a worse one, and across a whole sentence that chance
compounds. In a chat reply, the same behaviour is called *not being
repetitive*.

[The lesson generalises past translation: decoding parameters are not model
settings, they are task settings]{.hl}, and copying a temperature from a chat
example into a translation pipeline is a way to lose fifteen BLEU without
touching the model.

### Beam search: the folklore is wrong here

The received wisdom is that quality *degrades* at large beam widths — the
"curse of beam search", where the model's highest-probability sequence turns
out to be a short, degenerate one. **This model does not show it.** BLEU rises
monotonically from beam 1 to beam 64, and the length ratio stays flat at
about 1.02, so nothing is collapsing.

What the data does show is severe diminishing returns:

```text
  beam 1 -> 2      +0.61 BLEU     for  1.3x the time
  beam 2 -> 64     +0.57 BLEU     for  7.0x the time
```

[One extra beam buys as much as the following sixty-two.]{.hl} Beam 4 is the
usual default and the table says why: past it you are paying linearly for
almost nothing. The absence of the curse is itself informative — Marian
normalises by length during search, which is exactly the fix the curse
literature proposed, so a model that ships with the fix does not exhibit the
disease.

### Length penalty moves BLEU without moving quality

The length penalty divides a hypothesis's score by its length raised to a
power, so a higher value tolerates longer output. Sweeping it while holding
everything else fixed:

```text
  lenpen 0.2 -> 2.0     BLEU  30.51 -> 29.25    a 1.26-point swing
                        chrF  58.30 -> 58.39    a 0.09-point swing
                        length ratio 1.007 -> 1.041
```

BLEU moves fourteen times as much as chrF, and it moves in lockstep with
output *length*. That is not a quality difference; it is BLEU's brevity
penalty and precision denominator responding to the number of words produced.
[If you tune the length penalty against BLEU you are tuning your system to
produce slightly short output]{.hl}, which is a real and common way to buy a
point of BLEU that no reader would notice.

## Why BLEU is worse than usual for Turkish {#sec-machine-translation-turkish}

"BLEU is unfair to morphologically rich languages" is repeated often enough
to be folklore. It is true, the mechanism is simple, and the size of the
effect is measurable — so here it is measured rather than asserted.

### The mechanism, in two numbers

Take the 3,000 professionally translated sentence pairs of newstest2016 and
count both sides:

```text
                    words        characters      median words/sentence
  Turkish          46,243           335,110              13
  English          59,661           341,494              18

  the same content needs   1.29x as many WORDS in English
  but only                 1.02x as many CHARACTERS
```

[The same meaning, essentially the same number of characters, and 29% more
word tokens in English.]{.hl} Turkish packs into suffixes what English spells
out as separate words: *evinizden* is *from your house*, one token against
three.

That is the whole mechanism. A word-level metric divides a sentence into
tokens and asks how many match. Turkish gives it 29% fewer tokens to work
with, so **each Turkish token is 1.29× as large a share of the score**, and
one wrong word costs proportionally more. A character-level metric sees
essentially the same amount of material in both languages — the 1.02 ratio —
so it has no such asymmetry.

### The mechanism, measured

Predictions are cheap; this one is testable. Take a *correct* translation —
the reference itself, which scores 100 — and introduce **exactly one
morpheme of error**, the same semantic error in both languages: locative
becomes ablative, *in X* becomes *from X*.

In Turkish that is a suffix: `İstanbul'da` → `İstanbul'dan`. To be certain the
edit is a suffix and not a corrupted stem, only words with an explicit
apostrophe were perturbed, where the morpheme boundary is unambiguous. In
English it is a preposition: `in` → `from`.

```text
                              BLEU      chrF     BLEU/chrF     n
  Turkish   X'da -> X'dan    -14.90    -3.05        4.89x      264
  English   'in' -> 'from'   -12.65    -5.34        2.37x      997
```

Three readings, in order of how surprising they are.

**BLEU punishes the Turkish error 1.18× as hard**, which is the 1.29 token
ratio showing up almost exactly where the arithmetic predicts. And the
comparison is if anything conservative: the Turkish sentences in this subset
have a median of 19 words against English's 24, and *shorter* sentences make
each token a larger share — so a fair length match would widen the gap, not
narrow it.

**chrF punishes the Turkish error only 0.57× as hard.** Changing `'da` to
`'dan` adds one character to an eleven-character word; changing `in` to
`from` replaces a two-character word with a four-character one. At the
character level the Turkish error is genuinely smaller, and chrF says so.

**The disagreement between the two metrics is more than twice as large in
Turkish** — 4.89× against 2.37×. This is the number that matters
operationally. In English, BLEU and chrF mostly agree about how bad an error
is; in Turkish they differ by a factor of five, so [which metric you chose
decides which system you ship]{.hl}.

::: {.column-margin}
This is why chrF was proposed [@popovic2015chrf] and why the WMT community
moved to character-level and neural metrics for morphologically rich
languages. It is also why comparing a Turkish BLEU score against an English
one — "our Turkish system gets 29 and our German system gets 34, so Turkish is
harder" — is not a valid comparison at all. The metric is measuring different
amounts of the sentence in each language.
:::

### The second problem: word order

Turkish word order is freer than English. The unmarked order is
subject-object-verb, but constituents move for emphasis, and several orders
are fully grammatical for the same sentence. English permits far less
movement.

The consequence for a word n-gram metric is the one @sec-machine-translation-eval
already showed: moving a phrase destroys every n-gram that crosses the move,
while leaving the meaning intact. A correct English paraphrase that reorders
one phrase scored **50.27**. In a language where reordering is a normal
stylistic choice rather than an occasional one, a translator's legitimate
variation is charged at that rate every time.

Both problems have the same fix and it is not a better n-gram metric: score
at the character level, and score with a model that was trained on human
judgements.

## LLMs as translators {#sec-machine-translation-llm}

A general-purpose model can translate without being asked to be a translator.
The question is not whether it works but what it costs and where it wins, so
here is the head-to-head: `qwen3.5:9b` prompted zero-shot against
`opus-mt-tc-big`, a 237M-parameter model that does nothing else, on the
identical 400 sentences.

```text
wmt16 tr-en                          BLEU    chrF   s/sentence
  opus-mt-tc-big   greedy           31.44   59.53      0.013
  opus-mt-tc-big   beam-4           32.33   60.08      0.024
  qwen3.5:9b       zero-shot        29.37   58.32      1.088
  copy the source (control)          2.09   21.11

wmt16 en-tr                          BLEU    chrF   s/sentence
  opus-mt-tc-big   greedy           22.50   56.70      0.016
  opus-mt-tc-big   beam-4           23.13   57.41      0.064
  qwen3.5:9b       zero-shot        17.10   53.67      2.620
  copy the source (control)          2.10   19.87
```

The control row is there because a metric you have not sanity-checked is a
metric you do not understand: leaving the source untranslated scores 2.09, so
the numbers above are measuring translation rather than incidental overlap.

Three things to take from this.

**The small dedicated model wins both directions.** 237M parameters beat 9B,
by 3 BLEU into English and by 6 into Turkish, at **45× to 100× the speed**. A
model trained on nothing but this language pair is very hard to beat on this
language pair.

**The gap is twice as large translating *into* Turkish.** That is the
asymmetry to expect and to check for: a general multilingual model has seen
far more English than Turkish, and generating a morphologically rich language
is harder than parsing one. [Never assume your MT quality is symmetric —
measure both directions.]{.hl}

**Both directions are harder into Turkish for everyone.** opus-mt drops from
32.33 to 23.13 when the target changes. Part of that is genuine difficulty and
part is @sec-machine-translation-turkish's measurement artefact: the same
quality of translation scores lower when the target language gives BLEU 29%
fewer tokens to match. chrF, which does not have that bias, drops far less —
60.08 to 57.41.

### What an LLM buys that the dedicated model cannot

The table makes the LLM look strictly worse. On sentence-level news
translation it is. The reasons to reach for one anyway are things this
benchmark cannot express, because WMT is a list of isolated sentences:

- **Document context.** A dedicated sentence-level model translates each
  sentence independently and so cannot resolve a pronoun whose antecedent was
  two sentences ago, or keep a consistent formality register across a page.
- **Terminology adherence.** Put the glossary in the prompt and the model
  will mostly follow it. Enforcing terminology in a dedicated model means
  constrained decoding or retraining.
- **Register and audience.** *Translate this formally, for a legal audience,
  keeping the second person plural* is an instruction, not a model.
- **Any pair, immediately.** There is no `opus-mt` for most of the pairs a
  real product needs, and no data to train one.

@vilar2023prompting is the systematic study of how much prompting choices
matter here; the short version is that examples in the prompt help, and that
the quality of the examples matters more than the number.

::: {.column-margin}
The practical architecture in 2026 is usually neither alone: a dedicated model
for volume, an LLM for the documents where context and terminology matter,
and a router in front. The cost table decides the split — 0.024 seconds
against 1.088 is not a rounding difference at scale, it is the difference
between one machine and forty.
:::

## Low-resource translation {#sec-machine-translation-lowresource}

Turkish–English is not low-resource; OPUS has millions of pairs. But most
translation problems that arrive in industry are: a language pair nobody
publishes data for, or — far more often — a *domain* nobody publishes data
for. Legal Turkish, clinical Turkish, and the internal vocabulary of one
company are each low-resource regardless of how much news text exists.

The resource that does exist is **monolingual target text**. You have your own
documents; you do not have their translations.

**Back-translation** [@sennrich2016improving] turns that into training data.
Train a rough system in the *reverse* direction, use it to translate your
monolingual target-language text into the source language, and add those
synthetic pairs to training with the synthetic side as *input*. The synthetic
source may be poor; it does not matter as much as you would expect, because
the model only has to learn to produce the target side, and the target side is
genuine human text.

That asymmetry is the whole trick and the reason it works: [the noisy half is
on the input, where the model is allowed to be robust, and the clean half is
on the output, where it is being taught what to write.]{.hl}

Two adjacent moves worth knowing:

- **Fine-tuning on in-domain pairs.** A few thousand genuine in-domain pairs
  usually beat a large amount of synthetic data. Collect them from translation
  memories before generating anything.
- **Terminology injection.** Domain adaptation frequently is not a fluency
  problem at all but a vocabulary one: the model translates *hisse* as *share*
  when your house style is *stock*. That is a constraint to enforce at
  decoding or in a prompt, not a reason to retrain — and it is where
  @sec-machine-translation-llm has a genuine advantage.

::: {.column-margin}
Terminology drift is the failure that gets a translation project cancelled,
and it is invisible to every metric in @sec-machine-translation-eval: the
model's word and your house word are both plausible translations, so BLEU
against a generic reference cannot see the difference. Measure it directly —
take your glossary, and count how often the system used your term.
:::

## Translate-train, translate-test, or neither {#sec-machine-translation-pipeline}

You have a task — classification, retrieval, extraction — in Turkish, and the
best model or the labelled data is in English. Three options, and the choice
is an error-propagation question rather than a modelling one.

| approach | what happens | where errors accumulate |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **[Translate-train](#gloss-translate-train){#term-translate-train .term-ref}** | translate the English training data into Turkish once, train a Turkish model | translation noise is baked into training, but the model sees it consistently and can partly learn around it |
| **[Translate-test](#gloss-translate-test){#term-translate-test .term-ref}** | keep the English model, translate every incoming Turkish input at inference | a translation error at request time is a wrong prediction, every time, with no chance to recover |
| **Neither** | a multilingual model applied directly (@sec-pretraining) | no translation error at all; whatever the multilingual model gives up on Turkish |

: Three pipelines, three failure profiles {tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

::: {#gloss-translate-train .column-margin .term-gloss}
**translate-train** — machine-translate the labelled training data into the
target language, then train there. The translation cost is paid once, offline,
and the noise it introduces is at least consistent.
[↩](#term-translate-train){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-translate-test .column-margin .term-gloss}
**translate-test** — keep the model in its original language and translate
each incoming request into it. Nothing to retrain, and every user-facing
prediction now depends on a translation you did not check.
[↩](#term-translate-test){.term-back}
:::

The arithmetic that decides it: **translate-test pays the translation cost per
request, forever, and inherits the translation's error rate on every
prediction.** Translate-train pays once. If your system is a chatbot handling
a thousand requests a second, that is not a close call.

Two more considerations that decide it in practice:

1. **Which direction is your MT better in?** They are not symmetric. Measure
   both before assuming.
2. **What is the task?** Translate-test destroys anything that depends on
   surface form — @sec-sequence-labeling's span offsets do not survive
   translation, so extraction cannot use it at all. Document classification
   survives it comparatively well.

@sec-turkish-nlp gives the verdict for Turkish specifically, with numbers.
This chapter's contribution is the mechanics and the arithmetic; the two
should not be read as competing.

## Intuition checks {#sec-machine-translation-intuition}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your Turkish system scores 23 BLEU and your German one scores 34. Is Turkish harder?

You cannot conclude that, because BLEU is not measuring the same amount of
each sentence in the two languages. Turkish expresses the same content in 29%
fewer word tokens than English, so a word n-gram metric has fewer slots to
match and each error costs more of the score.

Measured here: the *same* semantic error — locative to ablative — costs
14.90 BLEU in Turkish and 12.65 in English. Some of your nine-point gap is
the metric.

Report chrF, which sees essentially the same amount of material in both
languages (a 1.02 character ratio against a 1.29 word ratio), and a neural
metric. Then compare.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. You copy the temperature from your chat pipeline into your translation pipeline. What happens?

You lose about half your quality. Measured on the same model and sentences:
beam-4 scores **30.17** BLEU, temperature 1.0 sampling scores **14.34**.

Translation has approximately one right answer and you want the
highest-probability sequence. Sampling deliberately introduces variation, and
across a sentence the chances of taking a worse token compound. The setting
that makes a chat reply feel natural makes a translation wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Is a wider beam worth it?

Almost never past 4. On this model, going from beam 1 to beam 2 buys +0.61
BLEU; going from beam 2 all the way to beam 64 buys +0.57 more, for seven
times the compute.

And check the folklore before repeating it: the "curse of beam search", where
quality *degrades* at large widths, does not appear here at all — BLEU rises
monotonically to 64 and the length ratio stays flat. Marian normalises by
length during search, which is the fix the curse literature proposed, so a
model that ships with the fix does not show the disease.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your BLEU went up 1.2 points after you tuned the length penalty. Did the system improve?

Probably not. Sweeping the length penalty from 0.2 to 2.0 moves BLEU by 1.26
points and chrF by 0.09, while the output length ratio moves from 1.007 to
1.041.

BLEU is responding to how many words you produced, through its brevity
penalty and its precision denominator. Tuning against it teaches your system
to be slightly terse. If a change moves BLEU and leaves chrF flat, you have
found a metric artefact, not an improvement.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. A 9B LLM or a 237M dedicated model?

Measured, on identical sentences: the dedicated model wins by 3 BLEU into
English and 6 into Turkish, at 45–100× the speed. On sentence-level news
translation there is no contest.

Reach for the LLM when the benchmark cannot express what you need: document
context for pronouns and register, a glossary in the prompt, a language pair
nobody publishes a model for. Those are real and this table cannot show them —
WMT is a list of isolated sentences.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Translate-train or translate-test?

Translate-test pays the translation cost on every request forever and turns
every translation error into a wrong prediction. Translate-train pays once,
offline, and the noise at least arrives consistently so the model can partly
learn around it.

Two things decide the rest: which direction your MT is actually better in —
measure, they are not symmetric — and whether your task depends on surface
form. Span extraction cannot survive translate-test at all, because the
offsets do not transfer. Document classification survives it comparatively
well.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-machine-translation-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the task

**Q: Why did attention get invented for translation and not for something else?**

Because the encoder-decoder RNN compressed the entire source into one
fixed-length vector, and translation makes that bottleneck obvious: quality
collapsed as sentences got longer, in the specific pattern of translating the
start and then drifting. Attention removed the compression by keeping one
vector per source token. Say also *why it fit*: translation has
output-to-input correspondence, so a weighted average that can concentrate on
one source position is the right interface — which is why early attention maps
looked like word alignments and why the same reading of a deep language model
does not hold up.

**Q: What does BLEU actually compute?**

Modified n-gram precision for n = 1 to 4, geometric mean, times a brevity
penalty. Be able to work an example. Then say what it cannot see: any correct
paraphrase, any reordering, and — by default — anything that differs in case.
A correct English translation that moves one phrase scores 50.

**Q: When would you not report BLEU?**

Never — report it, because comparability matters and its absence looks
evasive. The question is what you report *with* it. For a morphologically rich
target, chrF, because it gives partial credit for a right stem with a wrong
suffix. And a neural metric, because it is the only one of the family that
sees meaning. Ranking systems on BLEU alone is the failure.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Your MT quality dropped after a model upgrade, but only for one
customer. Debug it.**

Almost certainly terminology, not quality. Their house vocabulary changed
under them — the new model translates their term differently — and no
reference-based metric can see it, because both words are valid translations.
Measure it directly: take their glossary and count adherence. Then fix it at
decoding or in a prompt, not by retraining.

**Q: You need translation for 40 language pairs and have a budget.**

Route. A dedicated model per pair where one exists and volume justifies it,
an LLM for the long tail and for documents needing context or terminology
control. The number that decides the split is latency-per-sentence: measured
here, 0.024 seconds against 1.088 is the difference between one machine and
forty. Say also that you would measure both directions separately, because
they are not symmetric — 32.33 out of Turkish against 23.13 into it, on the
same model and corpus.

**Q: How would you build MT for a domain with no parallel data?**

Back-translation, and be able to say why it works: train a rough
reverse-direction system, use it to translate your monolingual *target* text
into the source, and train on those pairs with the synthetic side as input.
The noisy half is on the input, where robustness is expected, and the clean
human half is on the output, where the model is being taught what to write.
Then say what you would try first, which is finding a few thousand genuine
in-domain pairs in a translation memory — they usually beat a large amount of
synthetic data.

## Lab: build and evaluate a Turkish–English pipeline {#sec-machine-translation-lab}

Pick a domain you have text for — your own documents, a public corpus in your
field, product descriptions, support tickets. You need about 100 source
sentences and, for the evaluation half, 30 with human translations. Producing
those 30 yourself is part of the lab.

### Step 1 — name the test set, before anything else

Write down exactly which sentences you are evaluating on and where they came
from. If you use a public set, name it the way `sacrebleu` does. Half the
irreproducible MT results in the world are irreproducible because this step
was skipped.

### Step 2 — translate with a dedicated model, both directions

`opus-mt-tc-big-tr-en` and `-en-tr`, beam 4. Record seconds per sentence.
Report BLEU **with its signature** and chrF. The two directions will not
match; note the gap before you read @sec-machine-translation-turkish's
explanation of how much of it is the metric.

### Step 3 — translate with an LLM, same sentences

Put your glossary in the prompt, if you have one. Record seconds and tokens
per sentence, because this is where the cost argument gets made.

### Step 4 — the control

Score the *untranslated source* against the reference. It should be near zero.
If it is not, your metric is picking up something other than translation
quality — shared proper nouns, numbers, or a language pair closer than you
thought — and every number above needs re-reading.

### Step 5 — sweep the decoder

Beam 1, 4, 16, and sampling at temperature 0.7. Plot BLEU against seconds per
sentence. You are reproducing @sec-machine-translation-decoding's table on
your own data, and the question is where *your* curve flattens.

### Step 6 — read twenty outputs

Properly, side by side with the source. Rank the two systems yourself before
looking at the scores again. Then find one sentence where your ranking and
BLEU's disagree, and write down which of the two was wrong and why.

### Step 7 — measure terminology, if you have a glossary

For each glossary term, count how often each system used your word rather than
a synonym. This is the number that decides a real localisation project and it
appears in none of the metrics above.

### What to hand in

One table — systems against BLEU, chrF, seconds per sentence, terminology
adherence — plus the twenty-sentence reading, the disagreement you found, and
a paragraph on which system you would ship and at what volume the answer
changes.

## Exercises {#sec-machine-translation-exercises}

1. **BLEU by hand.** Compute BLEU for one sentence pair with a calculator,
   then check against `sacrebleu`. Now change one inflectional suffix in the
   candidate and recompute. Report how much BLEU moved, how much chrF moved,
   and whether the meaning moved as much as either.

2. **The reordering tax.** Take a correct translation and move one phrase to a
   different legal position. Compute BLEU before and after. Then do it in
   Turkish, where reordering is more freely available, and compare the two
   penalties.

3. **Find the curse, or fail to.** Sweep beam width from 1 to 128 on a model
   of your choice and plot BLEU and output length. If quality degrades, say at
   what width; if it does not, find out whether your model normalises by
   length during search.

4. **Length-penalty artefact.** Tune the length penalty to maximise BLEU on a
   development set. Report the BLEU gain, the chrF gain, and the change in
   output length ratio. Decide whether you would ship the tuned value.

5. **Direction asymmetry.** Measure the same model family in both directions
   on the same corpus. Explain how much of the gap is difficulty and how much
   is @sec-machine-translation-turkish's metric effect, using the word and
   character ratios of your own data.

6. **Back-translate something.** Take 2,000 monolingual sentences in your
   domain, translate them into the source language with an off-the-shelf
   model, and fine-tune on the synthetic pairs. Report the change on a genuine
   held-out set — and check whether it helped on the domain and hurt off it.

7. **Translate-test error propagation.** Take a classification task, translate
   the test inputs, and measure accuracy. Then hand-check the ten
   misclassified documents: how many are model errors and how many are
   translation errors? That ratio is the argument for or against the pipeline.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-mt-deeper}

First, print your BLEU signature. If you cannot say which tokenizer, casing
and smoothing produced a number, that number cannot be compared to anyone
else's — which is the entire argument of @post2018call.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [`sacrebleu`](https://github.com/mjpost/sacrebleu) | the reference implementation and the signature mechanism; also the easiest way to get chrF and TER right |
| [OPUS-MT](https://github.com/Helsinki-NLP/Opus-MT) | the dedicated models that beat a 9B LLM in this chapter, with training recipes published |
| [Stanford CS224N](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/) | the machine-translation lectures, including attention derived from the MT problem it was invented for |
| [The Annotated Transformer](https://nlp.seas.harvard.edu/annotated-transformer/) | the architecture as runnable code, written around a translation task |
| [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/) | every WMT findings paper, free — the shared-task reports are the honest state of the field each year |

| [Coding a Transformer from scratch in PyTorch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ISNdQcPhsts) — Umar Jamil | builds encoder–decoder translation end to end, which is the architecture this chapter's dedicated models still use |

## What to remember {#sec-machine-translation-summary}

- **Attention was a repair to a translation bug.** The encoder-decoder RNN
  squeezed a whole sentence into one fixed vector, quality collapsed on long
  sentences, and keeping one vector per source token fixed it. The
  architecture that now runs everything started there.

- **BLEU gives a correct translation 50.27** when it moves one phrase and
  differs in case on two words. It is modified n-gram precision with a brevity
  penalty and nothing more; it cannot see paraphrase, reordering, or meaning.
  Report it, never rank on it alone, and always report its signature.

- **The Turkish penalty is real and it is 1.29.** The same content needs 1.29×
  as many word tokens in English but only 1.02× as many characters, so a word
  n-gram metric has 29% fewer slots in Turkish and each error costs
  proportionally more. Measured on the same semantic error in both languages:
  BLEU charges **14.90** in Turkish against **12.65** in English, while chrF
  charges **3.05** against **5.34**. The two metrics disagree **4.89×** in
  Turkish and **2.37×** in English — which is why the metric you choose decides
  which system you ship.

- **Never compare BLEU across languages.** "Turkish scores 23 and German 34"
  is not a statement about difficulty; the metric is measuring different
  fractions of each sentence.

- **Decoding parameters are task settings, not model settings.** Beam 4 scores
  **30.17**; temperature 1.0 sampling scores **14.34** on the same model and
  sentences. The setting that makes chat feel natural halves a translator.

- **Check folklore before repeating it.** The "curse of beam search" did not
  appear here at all — BLEU rose monotonically to beam 64 with a flat length
  ratio. What did appear is brutal diminishing returns: beam 1→2 buys +0.61,
  beam 2→64 buys +0.57 for seven times the compute.

- **A BLEU gain with a flat chrF is a metric artefact.** Sweeping the length
  penalty moves BLEU 1.26 points and chrF 0.09, tracking output length. Tuning
  against BLEU teaches your system to be terse.

- **A 237M dedicated model beat a 9B LLM in both directions**, by 3 BLEU into
  English and 6 into Turkish, at 45–100× the speed. Reach for the LLM when you
  need what the benchmark cannot express: document context, glossary
  adherence, register, or a pair nobody publishes a model for.

- **Measure both directions.** 32.33 out of Turkish, 23.13 into it, same model
  family and corpus. MT quality is never symmetric and the asymmetry decides
  pipeline design.

- **Translate-test pays forever and translate-train pays once.** And
  translate-test cannot be used at all for anything that depends on surface
  form — span offsets do not survive translation.
